questions.stem: Which statement is part of cell theory?
options: All living things are made of identical cells
All living things are made of one or more cells
All cells contain a nucleus and many mitochondria
All cells are able to carry out photosynthesis
questions.explanation: Cell theory states that all living things are made of cells, the cell is the basic unit of life, and cells come from pre-existing cells. Bacterial cells have no nucleus or mitochondria, and only some cells photosynthesise.

questions.stem: Lipids are an important input for cells. Which is a major role of lipids in all cells?
options: Speeding up chemical reactions as catalysts
Making up the rigid cell wall of plant cells
Forming the bilayer of the plasma membrane
Carrying genetic information to the next cell
questions.explanation: Phospholipids form the bilayer that makes up the plasma membrane and the membranes of organelles; fats also store energy. Genetic information is carried by nucleic acids, catalysts are enzymes (proteins), and plant cell walls are made of cellulose, a carbohydrate.

questions.stem: Which pairing of a biological molecule and one of its roles is correct?
options: Lipid: glycogen, which stores energy in animal liver
Carbohydrate: haemoglobin, which carries oxygen in blood
Carbohydrate: cellulose, which makes up plant cell walls
Protein: starch, which stores energy in plant cells
questions.explanation: Cellulose is a carbohydrate that forms plant cell walls. Starch and glycogen are also carbohydrates, not a protein or a lipid, and haemoglobin is a protein.

questions.stem: Why do cells need vitamins, even though they are required only in small amounts?
options: Vitamins are the main fuel broken down to release energy
Vitamins are the building blocks joined to make proteins
Vitamins form the main structure of the plasma membrane itself
Many vitamins help enzymes work, so reactions slow without them
questions.explanation: Many vitamins act with enzymes, helping them catalyse reactions, so only small amounts are needed but a shortage disrupts metabolism. Energy comes mainly from carbohydrates and fats, and proteins are built from amino acids.

questions.stem: Which list contains only outputs released by an animal cell carrying out its normal processes?
options: Carbon dioxide and nitrogen-containing wastes such as urea
Oxygen and glucose made from carbon dioxide and water
Amino acids and fatty acids absorbed from the surrounding blood
Vitamins and minerals taken in to support enzymes
questions.explanation: Animal cells release carbon dioxide from respiration and nitrogen-containing wastes from breaking down amino acids. They do not photosynthesise, so they do not release oxygen or make glucose, and amino acids, vitamins and minerals are inputs.

questions.stem: Which feature do prokaryotic cells lack?
options: DNA
A membrane-bound nucleus
A surrounding plasma membrane
Ribosomes
questions.explanation: Prokaryotes, such as bacteria, have no nucleus or other membrane-bound organelles; their DNA lies in the cytoplasm. All cells have a plasma membrane, ribosomes and DNA.

questions.stem: A cell is about 2 µm long, has a cell wall, ribosomes and a single circular chromosome in the cytoplasm, and has no membrane-bound organelles. What type of cell is it?
options: A fungal cell such as a yeast cell
An animal cell such as a white blood cell
A prokaryotic cell such as a bacterium
A plant cell from the leaf of a moss
questions.explanation: Small size, a circular chromosome free in the cytoplasm and no membrane-bound organelles identify a prokaryote. Plant and fungal cells also have cell walls, but they are eukaryotic with a nucleus and organelles.

questions.stem: Which feature is found in both prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells?
options: Golgi bodies for packaging proteins
Ribosomes for making proteins
Mitochondria for respiration
A nucleus enclosing the DNA
questions.explanation: All cells make proteins, so all have ribosomes. Mitochondria, nuclei and Golgi bodies are membrane-bound structures found only in eukaryotic cells.

questions.stem: A student says bacteria cannot carry out aerobic respiration because they have no mitochondria. Which evaluation is correct?
options: Correct: bacteria release energy only by photosynthesis in the cytoplasm
Incorrect: many bacteria respire aerobically using enzymes on their plasma membrane
Correct: aerobic respiration can only take place inside a mitochondrion
Incorrect: bacteria have mitochondria, but they are too small to see
questions.explanation: Many bacteria respire aerobically; the reactions that happen in mitochondria in eukaryotes take place on the bacterial plasma membrane and in the cytoplasm. Prokaryotes have no mitochondria at all, however small.

questions.stem: In a eukaryotic cell, aerobic respiration takes place mainly in which organelle?
options: Golgi apparatus
Mitochondrion
Ribosome
Chloroplast
questions.explanation: Mitochondria release usable energy as ATP through aerobic respiration. Chloroplasts carry out photosynthesis, ribosomes make proteins, and the Golgi body packages them.

questions.stem: What is the main function of the nucleus?
options: It packages proteins into vesicles for export
It digests worn-out organelles and engulfed bacteria
It holds the DNA and controls the cell's activities
It releases energy by breaking down glucose
questions.explanation: The nucleus contains the cell's DNA, which carries the instructions controlling the cell. Energy release is the job of mitochondria, packaging of the Golgi body, and digestion of lysosomes.

questions.stem: Which set of structures would identify a cell as a plant cell rather than an animal cell?
options: Cell wall, chloroplasts and a large permanent vacuole
Mitochondria, ribosomes and a large central nucleus
Plasma membrane, cytoplasm and endoplasmic reticulum
Lysosomes, Golgi bodies and a single long flagellum
questions.explanation: Plant cells have a cellulose cell wall, chloroplasts for photosynthesis and a large vacuole. Both plant and animal cells have mitochondria, ribosomes, a nucleus, a plasma membrane and endoplasmic reticulum.

questions.stem: Cells in the pancreas make and release large amounts of digestive enzymes. Which organelles would be especially abundant in them?
options: Ribosomes, rough endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi bodies
Chloroplasts, vacuoles and a thick cellulose cell wall
Lysosomes, cilia and a large permanent central vacuole
Smooth endoplasmic reticulum and many stored fat droplets
questions.explanation: Enzymes are proteins: ribosomes on the rough ER make them, and Golgi bodies package them into vesicles for release. Animal cells have no chloroplasts or cell wall.

questions.stem: What is the role of lysosomes?
options: They contain enzymes that break down worn-out organelles and engulfed material
They contain chlorophyll that absorbs light energy for photosynthesis
They make proteins by joining amino acids in the order set by mRNA
They store water and dissolved substances and keep the cell firm
questions.explanation: Lysosomes are membrane sacs of digestive enzymes that break down old organelles and material taken in by the cell. Storing water and keeping a plant cell firm is the role of the vacuole.

questions.stem: Muscle cells in the legs of a long-distance runner contain far more mitochondria than skin cells do. Which explanation is best?
options: Muscle cells store more glucose, and mitochondria are the organelles that store it
Muscle cells divide more often, and mitochondria control cell division
Muscle cells need much more ATP for contraction, which mitochondria supply
Muscle cells need more protein, and mitochondria are the site of protein synthesis
questions.explanation: Contraction uses a lot of ATP, made by aerobic respiration in mitochondria, so active cells have many. Proteins are made at ribosomes, and glucose is stored as glycogen in the cytoplasm, not in mitochondria.

questions.stem: Why is it an advantage for eukaryotic cells to have internal compartments such as organelles?
options: The cell can remove its need for a plasma membrane around the outside
Organelles let the cell take in substances without any concentration gradient at all
Different reactions can take place in separate places with their own conditions
The cell can make its DNA without needing any enzymes in the cytoplasm
questions.explanation: Membrane-bound compartments keep reactions and their enzymes apart, so each can have suitable conditions, for example the acidic interior of a lysosome. Cells still need a plasma membrane and enzymes.

questions.stem: What is the plasma membrane mainly made of?
options: A layer of cellulose fibres with lipids between them
A double layer of proteins with DNA scattered through it
A single layer of starch with carbohydrate chains attached
A bilayer of phospholipids with proteins embedded in it
questions.explanation: The plasma membrane is a phospholipid bilayer with proteins embedded in and on it. Cellulose forms the plant cell wall, outside the membrane.

questions.stem: Why is the plasma membrane described as semi-permeable?
options: It lets substances cross only when energy is used
It lets some substances cross but not others
It lets all substances cross at the same rate
It is permeable only on one half of the cell
questions.explanation: A semi-permeable (selectively permeable) membrane allows some substances, such as water, oxygen and carbon dioxide, to cross while blocking others, such as large molecules. This controls exchange between the cell and its surroundings.

questions.stem: Which substance diffuses most easily straight through the phospholipid bilayer?
options: Glucose
Sodium ions
Starch
Oxygen
questions.explanation: Small, uncharged molecules such as oxygen and carbon dioxide pass straight through the lipid bilayer. Charged ions and larger molecules such as glucose cannot cross the bilayer easily, and starch is far too large.

questions.stem: Red food colouring is added to water around some cells. The colouring stays outside the cells, but oxygen in the water enters them. What does this show about the plasma membrane?
options: It is impermeable, so substances can enter only through the cell wall
It lets substances in only when the cell is actively dividing
It separates the cell from its surroundings and controls what enters
It is fully permeable, so all dissolved substances pass through it
questions.explanation: Some substances cross and others do not, showing the membrane is a selective boundary between the cell and its environment. A fully permeable membrane would let the colouring in too.

questions.stem: What is simple diffusion?
options: Net movement of particles from lower to higher concentration, using ATP energy
Movement of water only across a membrane towards a lower solute concentration
Movement of large particles into a cell by being surrounded by the membrane
Net movement of particles from higher to lower concentration, without using energy
questions.explanation: Diffusion is the passive net movement of particles down a concentration gradient, from high to low concentration, caused by their random motion. Movement against a gradient using ATP is active transport.

questions.stem: In the lungs, oxygen moves from the air in the alveoli into the blood. Which change would increase the rate of this diffusion?
options: Reducing the area of the surface across which gas is exchanged
Lowering the temperature of the air entering the lungs greatly
Increasing the difference in oxygen concentration between air and blood
Making the barrier between the air and the blood twice as thick
questions.explanation: The rate of diffusion increases with a steeper concentration gradient, a larger surface area, a thinner barrier and a higher temperature. A thicker barrier or smaller area would slow it.

questions.stem: A drop of dye is placed in still water at 10 °C and an identical drop in still water at 30 °C. Which result and reason are correct?
options: The dye spreads faster at 30 °C because warm water uses energy to pump particles
The dye spreads faster at 30 °C because particles move faster at higher temperature
The dye spreads faster at 10 °C because colder water is denser and pushes particles
The dye spreads at the same rate because the concentration gradient is the same
questions.explanation: Diffusion is driven by the random motion of particles, which is faster at higher temperatures, so the dye spreads more quickly in warmer water. No pumping or energy input is involved.

questions.stem: Which definition of osmosis is correct?
options: Net movement of solute across a semi-permeable membrane towards a higher water concentration
Net movement of water across a semi-permeable membrane towards a lower solute concentration
Net movement of any particle across a fully permeable membrane using ATP energy
Net movement of water across a semi-permeable membrane towards a higher solute concentration
questions.explanation: In osmosis water moves across a semi-permeable membrane from a dilute solution (more free water) to a more concentrated solution (less free water). It is passive and involves water, not solute.

questions.stem: Red blood cells are placed in pure water. What happens and why?
options: Nothing happens because the cells are isotonic with water
Water enters by osmosis until the cells swell and burst
Water leaves by osmosis and the cells shrink and shrivel
Salt leaves by diffusion and the cells stay the same size
questions.explanation: The cell contents have a higher solute concentration than pure water, so water moves in by osmosis. Animal cells have no cell wall to resist the pressure, so they swell and burst.

questions.stem: A plant cell is placed in a concentrated salt solution. What is seen under the microscope after some time?
options: The vacuole swells and presses hard against the cell wall
The salt enters the cell and it stays exactly the same size
The cytoplasm shrinks away from the cell wall as water leaves
The cell wall bursts as water enters the cell by osmosis
questions.explanation: The salt solution has a higher solute concentration than the cell sap, so water leaves by osmosis, the vacuole shrinks and the cytoplasm pulls away from the wall (plasmolysis). The wall itself does not burst.

questions.stem: Why does a plant cell in pure water become firm (turgid) but not burst, while an animal cell in pure water bursts?
options: The plant cell has no vacuole, so it cannot take in water
The plant cell's wall resists expansion as water enters
The plant cell's membrane is impermeable to water
The plant cell actively pumps out all the water it gains
questions.explanation: Both cells gain water by osmosis, but the rigid cellulose wall of the plant cell pushes back as the cell swells, so it becomes turgid instead of bursting. Plant cell membranes are permeable to water.

questions.stem: Potato cylinders were placed in sucrose solutions for an hour. Percentage change in mass: 0.0 M, +12; 0.2 M, +4; 0.4 M, −5; 0.6 M, −13. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: The potato cells have a solute concentration between 0.2 M and 0.4 M
The potato cells have a solute concentration higher than 0.6 M
Water left the cylinders in every solution, but most at 0.6 M
Sucrose entered the cylinders and caused all of the mass changes
questions.explanation: Cylinders gained mass where the solution was more dilute than the cells and lost mass where it was more concentrated, so no change would occur between 0.2 M and 0.4 M. The mass changes are due to water moving by osmosis.

questions.stem: In an osmosis practical, why do students record percentage change in mass rather than the change in grams?
options: Balances can only record changes in mass as percentages of the start
Percentages show the solute concentration of the potato cells directly
The cylinders start at slightly different masses, so percentages allow fair comparison
Percentages remove the need to dry the cylinders before they are weighed
questions.explanation: A heavier cylinder gains or loses more grams for the same osmotic effect, so dividing by the starting mass makes results comparable. Cylinders still need blotting dry before weighing.

questions.stem: What is the surface area to volume ratio of a cube-shaped cell with sides of 2 µm?
questions.explanation: Surface area = 6 × 2 × 2 = 24 µm²; volume = 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 µm³. The ratio is 24 : 8 = 3 : 1. A 1 µm cube has 6 : 1.

questions.stem: As a cell grows larger, what happens to its surface area to volume ratio?
options: It decreases, because volume increases faster than surface area
It increases, because surface area increases faster than volume
It stays the same, because both increase at the same rate
It decreases, because the surface area becomes smaller
questions.explanation: Surface area increases with the square of the length but volume with the cube, so the ratio falls as a cell grows. The surface area still increases, just more slowly than the volume.

questions.stem: What best explains why most cells are microscopic?
options: A small cell has fewer organelles, so it needs far fewer substances from outside
A small cell has a large surface area to volume ratio, so exchange can meet its needs
A small cell has a small surface area to volume ratio, so it loses less heat
A small cell needs no plasma membrane, because substances reach the centre quickly
questions.explanation: Materials enter and leave across the surface, but are used throughout the volume. A small cell has enough surface for its volume, and short diffusion distances to its centre. In a large cell the surface could not supply the volume fast enough.

questions.stem: Agar cubes of side 1 cm, 2 cm and 3 cm contain an indicator that changes colour when acid enters. They are placed in acid for 5 minutes. Which result is expected?
options: All three cubes have the same proportion of their volume changed in colour
Only the 3 cm cube changes colour, because it has the most surface area
The 1 cm cube has the largest proportion of its volume changed in colour
The 3 cm cube has the largest proportion of its volume changed in colour
questions.explanation: Acid diffuses in about the same distance from every surface, so the smallest cube, with the largest surface area to volume ratio (6 : 1, against 3 : 1 and 2 : 1), has the greatest proportion of its volume reached. This models why small cells exchange materials efficiently.

questions.stem: Some cells are long and thin or have a highly folded membrane, such as cells lining the small intestine with microvilli. How does this shape help them?
options: It increases the volume so that more organelles can fit inside
It reduces the surface area so that fewer harmful substances can get in
It increases the surface area to volume ratio, speeding exchange
It decreases the surface area to volume ratio, saving energy
questions.explanation: Folding or flattening a cell adds surface area without adding much volume, so the cell can exchange materials faster. Microvilli greatly increase the area for absorbing digested food.

questions.stem: A spherical single-celled organism doubles its diameter. Which statement about its exchange of materials is correct?
options: Its volume increases eight-fold but its surface area only four-fold
Its volume and its surface area both increase four-fold
Its surface area increases eight-fold but its volume only four-fold
Its volume doubles but its surface area stays the same
questions.explanation: Doubling the length of any shape multiplies surface area by 2² = 4 and volume by 2³ = 8, so the ratio halves. The cell has less surface for each unit of volume to exchange materials across.

questions.stem: Which statement about passive transport is correct?
options: It moves substances down a concentration gradient without using ATP
It moves substances against a concentration gradient using ATP
It moves only large particles such as whole bacteria into a cell
It happens only in plant cells that have a rigid cellulose cell wall
questions.explanation: Simple diffusion and osmosis are passive: particles move down a concentration gradient using their own kinetic energy, so the cell uses no ATP. They happen in all cells.
